*   **Analytical Inferences & Unresolved Storylines:** Corliss and Velez infer that private capital moves at high velocity while public stabilization funds lag behind administrative paperwork [9, 17, 21]. ============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Weight of Neutral By Noah Tan Colin Soria blew on his hands outside the Temescal laundromat, watching his breath hang in the air just long enough to be seen before vanishing. The security guard’s usual post-shift ritual—picking up takeout, maybe stopping by the bus shelter to chat with neighbors—had been pared down to just this: a quick errand, then home. "It’s not the kind of weather that stops you in your tracks," he said, nodding at the overcast sky. "Just that dull, gray blanket that makes everything feel a little slower." His rounds this week had been quieter, his head cold lingering like the fog from yesterday. Even the laundromat’s usual murmur of conversation had dimmed to the occasional rustle of turning pages.

Omar Lingio will tell you it's the fog. "It's moments like those that remind me why I love Temescal so much," he said. "I was just standing there, watching the fog roll in, and it felt like the whole neighborhood was wrapped in this quiet, peaceful blanket. The rest of the city might have been sunny and bustling, but here, it was like time stood still. I felt grateful to be a part of this community, to have my store here and be able to experience days like that." He's not wrong that the weather plays favorites with this block. It settles here when the rest of the city stays clear, like it's got an address to keep.

The fog and gray were all over the week, by the way. Noah Tan's pieces have Colin Soria blowing on his hands outside the laundromat, and the people he talked to called the weather "neutral" and "deliberate." I'll take the dull gray days as a small mercy. They gave the city a week to slow down and notice things. On the field, Simon Leary wrote the most careful column of the week about the A's. They are 1-0 and have won two straight, and there's a role change on the team that nobody has explained. I can't square 1-0 with two straight wins either, and I won't pretend to. Simon's restraint is right. A record is a beam, not a forecast. And over in Rockridge, Nia Rook found the neighborhood still lit up after Otis Redd's night on UNDOCKED, a 143-credit swing that has people arguing about who holds the edge and for how long. Rockridge, sitting at the top of the school table, can afford the entertainment. I won't begrudge anyone a good night.

That designation means the decision is made and the allocation mechanism is live. It does not yet mean the money has landed in the hands of the people it aims to stabilize—the renters, the long-term residents, the households that have held ground in West Oakland as the city has shifted around them. The fund was designed to keep people in their homes. Darius Clark, another bakery regular in the neighborhood, had absorbed the purpose. The A’s current record gives that idea its narrow footing: one lossless mark, two consecutive wins, and a role inside the team that is no longer quite where it was. The record is the beam.
